props.title: The Gnome-Mobile
props.initialSlug: Millionaire and kids help gnomes find new forest home

sections.content: Walt Disney's The Gnome-Mobile (1967) represents a fascinating entry in Disney's live-action fantasy period, following successful films like Mary Poppins (1964) and That Darn Cat! (1965). Starring Walter Brennan in a dual role as both D.J. Mulrooney and the gnome Knobby, the film showcases Disney's signature blend of practical effects and whimsical storytelling. Based on Upton Sinclair's novel "The Gnomobile," it's one of the rare instances where the acclaimed social realist author's work was adapted into family entertainment.

sections.content: The film fits into Disney's pattern of magical creature features from the 1960s-70s, alongside Darby O'Gill and the Little People (1959) and Bedknobs and Broomsticks (1971). These productions shared similar practical effects techniques, using forced perspective and carefully designed sets to create the illusion of size differences between human and magical characters. The Gnome-Mobile particularly excels in its innovative car sequences, where the titular vehicle appears to drive through massive redwood forests while carrying its tiny passengers.

The environmental message embedded in The Gnome-Mobile was ahead of its time, predating the mainstream ecological movement. Its story of protecting ancient redwood forests resonates with later environmental fantasy films like FernGully: The Last Rainforest (1992) and Epic (2013). The film's treatment of the logging industry, through D.J. Mulrooney's character arc, offers a nuanced take on conservation versus commerce that was unusual for children's entertainment of the era. sections.content: The success of The Gnome-Mobile influenced Disney's subsequent live-action fantasy productions, including Pete's Dragon (1977) and Return to Witch Mountain (1978). These films established a template for combining practical effects with family-friendly adventure that would continue through Honey, I Shrunk the Kids (1989) and beyond. The practical effects work by Peter Ellenshaw and Eustace Lycett set new standards for in-camera tricks that would influence fantasy filmmaking for decades.
